entries.response: A function does something when you call it. function totalSpend(transactions) { ... } names it and says what input it takes — transactions here is the list you're working with.
An array is a list of values in order. transactions[0] gets the first item, transactions.length tells you how many items there are in total.

entries.response: An object holds named fields. transactions[i].amount means 'the amount field of the i-th transaction' — the dot gets you the named value out.
Declare let total = 0; before the loop starts, then inside the loop do total += transactions[i].amount; — that adds each amount onto the running total as you go.
Check where let total = 0 is written — if it's inside the loop instead of before it, it resets to zero on every single pass, so you only ever end up with the last item's value.
for (let i = 0; i < transactions.length; i++) { ... } — using .length means the loop always covers the whole list, however many items it has.
Put an if check inside the loop before you add to the total — if (transactions[i].category === category) { total += transactions[i].amount; } — only matching items get added.
NaN usually means a typo in a property name — like transactions[i].amout instead of .amount — so it's trying to do maths on something that doesn't exist.

If the visible ledger test passes but the hidden one doesn't, that's usually a sign the number's been typed in directly rather than calculated — the function needs to work on any list it's given, not just this one.
